summary:
Savills research finds global demand for prime office space strengthening, with 58 percent of the largest prime office leasing deals in H1 2026 involving occupiers expanding their footprints. Only 5 percent involved space reduction, while relocations or renewals at broadly the same footprint fell from 44 percent in H2 2025 to 37 percent in H1 2026. Savills frames this as prime demand decoupling from the wider office market, as organisations invest in better buildings and locations rather than simply cutting property commitments.

Flexible workspace operators are the most expansionary group: 78 percent of the largest flex provider deals were expansions, and more than half of those involved taking additional space in markets where the operator already had a presence, suggesting deepening in selected cities rather than indiscriminate growth.

AI companies are an emerging demand source, accounting for 17 percent of prime office deals involving technology companies in H1 2026, up from 3 percent two years earlier. Every identified AI company transaction was an expansion. Demand clusters around established tech and innovation hubs led by San Francisco, with notable activity in Seattle and London's West End. Sarah Brooks of Savills World Research called the influence of AI and tech occupiers "unmistakable," citing long-term investment in flagship workplaces in San Francisco, London and Shenzhen to compete for talent and support client engagement and brand.

Costs are rising: Savills Prime Office Costs research shows net all-in costs (rent plus fit-out) up 1 percent globally in Q2 and 5.3 percent year on year. North America rose 2.1 percent versus 0.5 percent in EMEA and Asia Pacific. San Francisco jumped 7.7 percent, Downtown New York 5.6 percent, Washington DC 4 percent, Seoul 3.8 percent, Melbourne 3.6 percent. Rick Schuham noted some mainland Chinese markets show weaker demand and rising availability. Savills defines prime as the top tier of Grade A, typically the highest 5 to 10 percent of rents.
